analysis.one_liner: Opens U.S. nuclear exports to India by waiving decades-old nonproliferation law.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on this bill directly; instead it wrote the bill's text into a House bill that President Bush signed into law in December 2006, opening U.S. nuclear trade with India for the first time in decades.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill exempts U.S. exports of nuclear material, equipment, and technology to India from Atomic Energy Act requirements that currently block nuclear trade with countries that have built nuclear weapons outside the Nonproliferation Treaty. It keeps a ban on exporting uranium enrichment, spent-fuel reprocessing, and heavy-water technology to India, and requires the President to report regularly on whether India is living up to its nonproliferation commitments. A second title sets up U.S. procedures for international inspectors under an IAEA agreement covering the United States itself.
analysis.who_benefits: U.S. nuclear reactor manufacturers, fuel suppliers, and related companies gain access to India's civilian nuclear market, which has been closed to them since the 1970s. India's civil nuclear program gains fuel and equipment from the world's largest nuclear suppliers. The Bush administration gains a foreign-policy achievement in its strategic partnership with India.
analysis.who_benefits_short: U.S. nuclear suppliers and India's nuclear program

how_it_helps.text: Exempts a U.S.-India cooperation agreement from Atomic Energy Act requirements, including the rule requiring full IAEA safeguards on a country's peaceful nuclear program and rules that bar exports to states that acquired nuclear explosive devices after 1978, letting trade begin with a country that never joined the Nonproliferation Treaty.
Opens India's civilian nuclear market to U.S. suppliers while barring licenses for exports of uranium enrichment, spent-fuel reprocessing, or heavy-water technology to India, with narrow exceptions.

Requires the President to keep Congress informed of India's nuclear activities and to certify annually whether India is in full compliance with its nonproliferation commitments, with waivers void if India detonates a nuclear device.

analysis.who_pays: The cost is diffuse rather than a direct bill to taxpayers: the international nonproliferation system loses much of its leverage over India, which keeps producing nuclear weapons material in facilities outside international inspection while gaining the benefits of civilian nuclear trade. If India's conduct later falls short, the reporting requirements let Congress respond but do not automatically stop trade.

drawbacks.text: India keeps its military nuclear program and its production of weapons material outside international safeguards while receiving the trade benefits the law previously reserved for countries that had given up nuclear weapons, a break from the principle that nuclear trade requires full safeguards.

The bill's policy declarations, such as ending fissile-material production by India and Pakistan, are statements of policy rather than enforceable requirements, so they constrain future administrations only politically.

The Presidential waivers cover not just safeguards requirements but also export criteria and past sanctions under the Atomic Energy Act, meaning Congress set aside legal barriers it had previously treated as conditions for trade.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a concrete, large benefit to U.S. nuclear suppliers and to U.S.-India relations, and it does retain real limits, including a ban on exporting the most sensitive technologies and annual compliance reporting. The serious cost is strategic rather than financial: trading with India while it stays outside the Nonproliferation Treaty and outside safeguards on its weapons program weakens the standard the United States spent decades enforcing, and nonproliferation advocates argued the annual reporting does not make up for that. Whether the trade-off is worth it is a judgment about national strategy, not a hidden transfer, and the safeguards and reporting provisions in the bill were stronger than many critics feared.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate never passed S. 3709 as its own bill; on November 16, 2006 it laid the measure before the Senate by unanimous consent and wrote the bill's text into a House bill, H.R. 5682, which then passed both chambers and was signed by President Bush in December 2006.

narrative.text: The Senate Foreign Relations Committee, chaired by Senator Lugar, reported this as an original committee measure on July 20, 2006, and it was placed on the Senate calendar the same day.
On November 16, 2006, the Senate laid the measure before it by unanimous consent and incorporated the bill into H.R. 5682 as the Senate's amendment, then returned the original bill to the calendar.
H.R. 5682, containing this bill's text, passed both chambers and President George W. Bush signed it into law in December 2006 as the United States-India Peaceful Atomic Energy Cooperation Act.
The bill carried no cosponsors and no roll-call votes appear in its own record; the Senate acted on it by unanimous consent.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: U.S. nuclear reactor and fuel suppliers and India's civil nuclear program are the clear winners, since the law opened a large export market that had been closed since the 1970s; the Bush administration also gained its headline foreign-policy achievement with India.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: U.S. nuclear suppliers and India's nuclear program

for.name: Sen. Richard Lugar
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill as an original committee measure, had it placed on the Senate calendar, and brought it before the Senate on November 16, 2006.

for.name: U.S. Senate
for.role: Adopted the bill's text as its amendment to H.R. 5682
for.what_they_did: Laid the measure before the Senate by unanimous consent on November 16, 2006 and incorporated it into H.R. 5682.

for.name: President George W. Bush
for.what_they_did: Made the U.S.-India nuclear agreement a top foreign-policy priority after the July 2005 joint statement with India and signed the measure into law as part of H.R. 5682 in December 2006.

against.name: Rep. Edward Markey
against.role: House member and senior nonproliferation critic
against.what_they_did: Led opposition to the U.S.-India nuclear exemption in the House, arguing it rewarded a nuclear-armed state outside the Nonproliferation Treaty; he opposed the final H.R. 5682.

against.name: Arms Control Association
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed the deal, arguing that exempting India from Atomic Energy Act requirements weakened the nonproliferation standard applied to other countries.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows no party split: the bill had no cosponsors because Lugar reported it himself as an original measure, the Senate took it up by unanimous consent, and the final law passed both chambers with large bipartisan majorities.

industries.industry: U.S. nuclear reactor manufacturers and fuel suppliers
industries.note: The law reopens India's civilian nuclear market to U.S. reactor builders and fuel suppliers after roughly three decades of ban, creating a large new export business. Their gain depends on a policy that nonproliferation critics argue weakens the rules the U.S. asks every other country to follow, and the law does bar selling India the most sensitive fuel-cycle technology.

India gains access to world nuclear fuel and equipment without joining the Nonproliferation Treaty or placing its weapons program under safeguards, while accepting perpetual IAEA safeguards on its declared civilian facilities. Whether this serves ordinary people turns on whether the deal dampens or fuels a regional nuclear arms race.

The exemption sets aside Atomic Energy Act requirements, including full-safeguards and post-1978 acquisition rules, that were the legal backbone of U.S. nonproliferation enforcement, reducing the leverage the United States previously held over India. The bill compensates with end-use monitoring, annual certification, and a voiding clause if India tests a nuclear device.
